stories.headline: NASDAQ 100 TOPS 29,000 FOR THE FIRST TIME AS MEMORY-CHIP REBOUND POWERS A BROAD RALLY
stories.body: The Dow rose 385 points (+0.74%) to 52,224.64, the S&P 500 gained 0.89% to 7,509.20, and the Nasdaq 100 jumped 1.5% to 29,022 as a memory-led semiconductor rally - the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose about 5.2% - pushed the tech-heavy index past 29,000 for the first time. Micron surged roughly 10-12% and Sandisk soared 14% after Morgan Stanley predicted memory prices could rise 25% on sustained AI demand, while AMD added another 5-8% on top of its Microsoft AI deal gains.
stories.explain: This is a supply-side bet on the AI trade, not a broad risk-on move: DRAM and HBM are the specific inputs hyperscalers need for training clusters, so a bank forecasting a 25% memory-price increase is really forecasting that AI capex keeps converting into physical chip orders rather than staying a spending promise. That's why the rally concentrated so heavily in memory names - Micron, Sandisk - instead of spreading evenly across tech, and why it happened even as headlines about the Iran conflict kept running in the background.

stories.headline: OIL EXTENDS ITS CLIMB AS US STRIKES ON IRAN ENTER A 10TH DAY, BUT EQUITIES LOOK RIGHT THROUGH IT
stories.body: WTI rose to $84.29 a barrel (+2.2%) and Brent climbed to $91.10 (+2.1%) after a tanker carrying oil products was reportedly struck near the Strait of Hormuz and Washington carried out its 10th consecutive day of strikes on Iran, yet the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both rallied hard on the same session.
stories.explain: The equity market's ability to shrug off a rising war-risk premium in oil is itself informative: traders are pricing this as a contained, tradeable disruption to a single commodity rather than a threat to broader corporate earnings or global growth, which is why capital rotated into chip stocks instead of out of risk assets entirely. That divergence would break quickly if the conflict escalated into an actual chokepoint closure at Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global oil supply transits daily.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS BARELY BUDGE AS TRADERS LOOK PAST OIL AND CHIPS TO NEXT WEEK'S FOMC MEETING
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 0.6 basis points to 4.592% and the 2-year eased 1.1 basis points to 4.204%, holding a roughly 39-basis-point curve as investors turned toward the July 28-29 FOMC meeting - the second under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has called current prices 'too high' even as June's dot plot lifted the Fed's own year-end PCE inflation forecast to 3.6% from 2.7% in March.
stories.explain: Barely-there yield moves on a day with a 2%-plus oil spike and a 1.5% Nasdaq 100 rally signal that bond traders see both as noise relative to the one variable that actually matters to them right now: whether Warsh's Fed treats sticky inflation or a cooling labor market as the bigger risk next week. A hawkish surprise would need oil's gain to look durable rather than headline-driven, which today's whipsaw pattern in crude does not yet support.

stories.headline: BRAZIL'S 25% TARIFF HITS WEDNESDAY AS THE WHITE HOUSE TEASES MORE TRADE ACTION 'SOON'
stories.body: A 25% US tariff on most imports from Brazil takes effect Wednesday, July 22 - the first strike in what USTR has signaled will be a broader rollout after proposing Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% on roughly 60 countries and the EU over forced-labor findings, with the White House indicating Tuesday that additional trade actions are coming 'soon' as it works to rebuild a global tariff regime.
stories.explain: A tariff's economic incidence - who actually eats the 25% - splits between the foreign exporter (via a lower pre-tariff price), the US importer (via compressed margins), and the American consumer (via a higher shelf price), and the split is set by relative price elasticities on each side, not by who wrote the check to Customs. Brazil supplies a meaningful share of US coffee, orange juice and beef imports, categories where US buyers have limited fast substitutes, so economists expect more of this particular tariff to pass through to US prices than the incidence split typically seen in tariffs on goods with easy substitute suppliers.

stories.headline: GOLD HOLDS ABOVE $4,000 AS INVESTORS WEIGH WAR-RISK DEMAND AGAINST A STEADY DOLLAR AHEAD OF THE FED
stories.body: Gold rose to $4,083 an ounce (+1.9%), holding comfortably above the psychological $4,000 level as safe-haven buying tied to the Iran conflict outweighed a nearly flat US Dollar Index (100.92, -0.03%) heading into next week's FOMC decision.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its price is set by the tug-of-war between real demand for a hedge against war or inflation risk and the opportunity cost of holding a zero-coupon asset while Treasury yields sit near 4.6%. Today's gain despite a flat dollar and only marginally lower yields suggests the war-risk side of that trade is currently doing more work than the rates side - a dynamic that would likely reverse fast if next week's FOMC delivers a meaningfully hawkish surprise.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN AD WARDE MANUEL TO STEP DOWN AT YEAR-END AFTER MONTHS-LONG ATHLETICS DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION
stories.body: Michigan announced Monday that athletic director Warde Manuel will step down at the end of the calendar year following an internal investigation into the athletics department, a departure that comes despite national championships in both football and basketball on his watch and hands his successor the job of evaluating first-year men's basketball coach Mike Boynton, who signed a team-friendly two-year deal after Dusty May's late-offseason exit to the NBA.

stories.headline: PISTONS' CONTRACT TALKS WITH FREE AGENT CENTER JALEN DUREN REPORTEDLY AT A 'STANDSTILL'
stories.body: ESPN's Ramona Shelburne reported that Detroit's negotiations with restricted free agent Jalen Duren have stalled and could stretch deep into August, even as Pistons officials continue to call re-signing him the offseason's top priority after reshaping the roster around him - acquiring Taurean Prince and Gary Harris from Milwaukee for Caris LeVert, and re-signing forward Javonte Green to a one-year, $3.95 million deal.

stories.headline: TRAINING CAMPS OPEN LEAGUE-WIDE AS DOLPHINS, PACKERS LOCK UP DEFENSIVE STARTERS WITH NEW EXTENSIONS
stories.body: All 32 NFL teams are set to report to training camp by July 28 - the Cardinals and Panthers already underway ahead of the Aug. 6 Hall of Fame Game - as Miami signed linebacker Jordyn Brooks to a three-year, $51.3 million extension and Green Bay locked up defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt for three years and $57 million; Carolina's Taylor Moton will open camp on the reserve/NFI list after being diagnosed with a lung blood clot in June.

stories.headline: SEC MEDIA DAYS DAY TWO: KIRBY SMART'S GEORGIA TAKES THE TAMPA STAGE AS THE CONFERENCE OPENS ITS FIRST NINE-GAME SLATE
stories.body: Georgia's Kirby Smart headlined Tuesday's SEC Media Days session alongside Auburn's Alex Golesh, South Carolina's Shane Beamer and Vanderbilt's Clark Lea, with the conference kicking off a nine-game schedule for the first time as it chases a national title after two straight seasons without one; Lane Kiffin's first appearance as LSU's coach and Arch Manning's Texas spotlight are still ahead later in the week.

sports.detail: Jedd Fisch remains in a quiet recruiting period while calling plays himself after OC Jimmie Dougherty's February departure; 4-star WR commit Tre Moore has been turning heads at summer 7v7 events. Season opens with the Boeing Apple Cup vs. Washington State, Sunday, Sept. 6 (1 p.m. PT, NBC) at Husky Stadium.

Danny Sprinkle is rebuilding through the transfer portal after a 16-17 finish and Zoom Diallo's departure, landing Croatian forward Boris Tisma while continuing to pursue Rainier Beach's Jaylen Petty. Center Hannes Steinbach went 14th overall to Charlotte in the 2026 NBA Draft.

HBO dropped the trailer for 'Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the Seattle Seahawks' (premieres Aug. 11) as the defending Super Bowl champs opened camp; safety Nick Emmanwori was placed on the PUP list but a team source called it no major concern. NFL owners still expected to vote in August on the Khosla family's record $9.612 billion purchase.

Contract talks with free agent center Jalen Duren have reportedly hit a 'standstill' and could drag into August, even after Detroit freed cap space by sending Caris LeVert to Milwaukee for Taurean Prince and Gary Harris and re-signing Javonte Green for one year.

Seattle routed Cincinnati 8-0 Monday behind Cal Raleigh's sixth career grand slam and a three-hitter from George Kirby and the bullpen, improving to 51-50 and taking over first place in the AL West. Mariners close the series tonight, 9:40 p.m. PT at T-Mobile Park (Luis Castillo vs. Chase Burns).

watchlist: FOMC meets July 28-29 - the second meeting under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, whose June dot plot lifted the year-end PCE inflation forecast to 3.6%
Brazil's 25% US tariff takes effect Wednesday, July 22 - first move in a broader Section 301 rollout USTR has teased for weeks
Mariners close a home series vs. Reds tonight, 9:40 p.m. PT at T-Mobile Park - Seattle (51-50) just took first in the AL West
SEC Media Days run through Thursday in Tampa - Lane Kiffin's first LSU appearance and Arch Manning's Texas spotlight still ahead
Megacap tech earnings continue this week - will test whether today's memory-led Nasdaq 100 rally to 29,022 has legs

deepDive.title: Tariff Incidence: Who Actually Pays When a 25% Levy Hits Brazilian Imports?
content: Wednesday, a 25% US tariff on most goods from Brazil takes effect - the opening move in a broader Section 301 rollout that USTR has been signaling for weeks, with proposed duties of 10-12.5% still pending on roughly 60 more countries and the EU. It's tempting to read a tariff announcement as a straightforward tax on the foreign country named in the headline, but that's not how the economics actually work. The check gets written by the US importer at the border, and from there the cost of that 25% gets divided up between three parties - the Brazilian exporter, the US importer, and the American consumer - in shares that depend entirely on how substitutable the good is, not on which country's flag is on the press release.

That division is governed by relative price elasticities on each side of the transaction. If Brazilian exporters have few alternative buyers for their coffee or orange juice, they'll cut their pre-tariff price to keep US buyers from walking away, absorbing part of the cost themselves - that's a low elasticity of supply. If American consumers have easy substitutes - a different coffee origin, a domestic juice brand - retailers can't pass much of the tariff through without losing customers, so importers eat more of the margin hit themselves. The math works like a seesaw: whichever side can walk away more easily pays less, and the side that's stuck absorbs more.

Brazil is a useful case precisely because US buyers often can't walk away easily. The US imports a large share of its coffee, orange juice concentrate and beef from Brazil, and swapping to another origin takes time, contracts, and in some cases isn't possible at the volumes US roasters and beverage makers need. Economists who studied the 2018-2019 US-China tariffs found that nearly the full cost of those duties passed through to US import prices within months, because Chinese manufacturers had thinner margins to absorb losses and US buyers couldn't quickly resource elsewhere either - a similar dynamic is what analysts are watching for here.

That's the mechanism to watch as this rolls out this week: if Brazilian coffee and OJ futures barely move while US import prices for those goods jump close to the full 25%, that's the textbook high-pass-through outcome, and it will eventually show up as a small but real addition to headline CPI - a data point the Fed will be watching heading into next week's FOMC meeting, where Chair Warsh has already flagged inflation as 'too high.' If Brazilian producers instead cut prices meaningfully to hold onto US buyers, that tells you the elasticity story is more balanced than the coffee-and-OJ intuition suggests - and it's exactly the kind of granular, good-by-good pass-through data that turns a tariff headline into an actual inflation forecast.
